hero.subtitle: The hierarchical naming system that maps human-readable names to IP addresses

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) is a distributed, hierarchical naming system that translates human-readable domain names (like www.example.com) into IP addresses (like 93.184.216.34) and other resource records.

RFC 1034 defines the concepts behind DNS, while its companion RFC 1035 details the implementation. Together, they form the foundation of the Internet's naming infrastructure.

Before DNS, host name-to-address mappings were maintained in a single HOSTS.TXT file distributed to every machine. As the Internet grew, this approach became completely unmanageable.

sections.title: Domain Name Space
sections.content:
The domain name space is a tree structure where each node has a label up to 63 characters long. A domain name is the sequence of labels from a node to the root, separated by dots.

Root Domain
The root of the tree is represented by an empty label (or a trailing dot). The root zone is managed by IANA and served by 13 root server clusters (a.root-servers.net through m.root-servers.net).
Top-Level Domains (TLDs)
Direct children of the root include generic TLDs (.com, .org, .net) and country-code TLDs (.uk, .de, .jp). Each TLD is managed by a designated registry.
Zones and Delegation
The name space is divided into zones, each managed by a particular authority. A zone can delegate subdomains to other name servers, creating a distributed administration model.

A fully-qualified domain name (FQDN) includes the trailing dot representing the root: www.example.com. — though the trailing dot is usually omitted in everyday use.

sections.title: Name Servers
sections.content:
Name servers store DNS data and respond to queries. They are organized hierarchically, matching the structure of the domain name space.

Server Type
Role
Example
Root Server
Knows TLD authoritative servers
a.root-servers.net
TLD Server
Knows domain authoritative servers
a.gtld-servers.net
Authoritative
Holds actual DNS records for a zone
ns1.example.com
Recursive Resolver
Resolves queries on behalf of clients
8.8.8.8 (Google)

Each zone must have at least two authoritative name servers for redundancy. The primary server holds the master copy of zone data; secondary servers receive copies via zone transfers.

sections.title: Resolvers
sections.content:
Resolvers are the client side of DNS, responsible for translating application queries into the protocol messages needed to find answers.

Stub Resolver
A minimal resolver built into the operating system. It sends recursive queries to a configured DNS server and relies on that server to do the full resolution.
Recursive Resolver
A full-service resolver that follows the chain of delegations from root to authoritative server. It caches results to speed up future queries.
Iterative vs. Recursive
In iterative resolution, a server returns a referral to the next server to ask. In recursive resolution, the server takes full responsibility for finding the answer on behalf of the client.

sections.title: Caching
sections.content:
Caching is fundamental to DNS performance. Without caching, every DNS lookup would require traversing the hierarchy from root servers.

TTL (Time to Live)Each record has a TTL specifying how long it may be cached (in seconds)
Positive CachingSuccessful lookups are cached for the duration of the TTL
Negative CachingNXDOMAIN (name not found) results are also cached (RFC 2308)
Cache PoisoningAn attack where forged responses inject false entries into the cache

Setting TTL values involves a trade-off: low TTLs allow faster propagation of changes but increase query load on authoritative servers. High TTLs reduce load but make changes slow to propagate.

references.text: Mockapetris, P., "Domain Names - Implementation and Specification", RFC 1035, November 1987.
